title: Floor Malting and Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: How floor malting works step by step, why a few distilleries still do it and what it would take to floor malt barley in Indian heat.
teaser: Floor malting is slow, hot and hard on the back. It is also the oldest way to turn barley into whisky malt.
standfirst: Before industrial maltings, every distillery malted its own barley on a stone floor. A few still do, for part of their needs. Understanding floor malting teaches what malt really is, even if you will buy every kilo from a maltster.
sections: Malting turns barley into a sugar source

Raw barley holds its starch locked inside cell walls, with few enzymes to break it down. Malting persuades the grain to start growing, which builds enzymes and opens up the starch. Kilning then stops growth and dries the grain so it keeps. The result is malt that a distiller can mash into sugar. Our guide to malting for whisky versus malting for beer covers how the targets differ.

Floor malting is the traditional way to manage the growing stage: barley spread on a floor and turned by hand.

Barley is soaked in water in a steep tank, with wet periods alternating with air rests so the grain can breathe. Over about two days the moisture rises from around 12% to roughly 45%. That is the trigger for germination.

Water quality and temperature matter. Warm steep water speeds things up but also encourages microbes. Too long underwater and the grain suffocates.

The wet barley is spread across a malting floor, typically in a layer a few centimetres to a few tens of centimetres deep. Over around four to five days it germinates. Rootlets appear and the shoot, the acrospire, grows inside the husk.

Germination produces heat. Left alone, the bed warms up and the rootlets knot together into a mat. So maltsters turn the grain by hand with wooden shovels and rakes, several times a day, to release heat, add air and keep the rootlets apart. Bed depth is the control: spread thinner to cool it, pile deeper to warm it. Maltsters commonly aim to keep the grain in a cool range, around the mid to high teens in °C.

The floor detail that tells the story: the maltster judges readiness by rubbing a grain between finger and thumb. When the inside smears like chalk rather than feeling hard or doughy, the starch is ready, a test called rubbing out.

The green malt goes to a kiln, where warm air dries it. Moisture drops to around 4 to 5% and growth stops. Kilning starts gently to protect enzymes, then finishes hotter. If peat is burnt, it goes on early while the malt is still damp, because damp grain picks up smoke far more readily. Our guide to peat sources and smoke character covers that step.

After kilning, rootlets are removed and the malt rests before milling.
Why so few distilleries still do it

Floor malting is labour heavy and low output. A malting floor handles only a small batch at a time, takes nearly a week per batch and needs people turning grain around the clock. Industrial maltings with drums or germination boxes produce far more consistent malt at a fraction of the labour.

So the few distilleries that still floor malt usually do it for part of their barley, for heritage and for visitors as much as for flavour. Whether floor malt makes a better whisky is debated. Some distillers believe the slower, less even germination adds character. Others think the difference is lost once the spirit spends years in a cask.

Germinating barley wants cool air. Floor malting traditionally happened in cooler months in cool climates for that reason. In most Indian locations, ambient temperatures for much of the year sit well above the comfortable range for a germinating bed. The grain would run hot, grow too fast and lose extract to rootlets.

A floor malting in India would need either a cool season window, a climate controlled room or a hill site. Each brings cost. For most craft distilleries, the sensible route is buying good malt and learning to read its analysis. Our guide to how whisky is made shows where malt fits in the whole chain.
Learn malting even if you never do it

A distiller who understands steeping, germination and kilning reads a malt analysis differently. Low extract, high moisture or poor modification all have causes in the malt house. Knowing them helps you talk to your maltster and spot a bad lot before it costs you spirit. That understanding of raw materials is a core part of a structured distilling course.

Your first step: ask your maltster for the modification figures on your current malt and do the rubbing out test on a handful of grains from the sack.
faqs: It is the traditional way of germinating barley by spreading steeped grain on a floor and turning it by hand for several days before kilning.
How long does floor malting take?
Roughly a week: about two days of steeping, four to five days of germination on the floor and then kilning.
Does floor malted barley make better whisky?
It is debated. Some distillers believe it adds character. Others think any difference is small compared with fermentation, distillation and cask.
Can barley be floor malted in India?
Possible, but heat makes it hard. It would need a cool season, a climate controlled room or a cool hill site to keep the germinating grain from overheating.
